description: We are a team of grade 11 students passionate about space exploration, aerospace engineering, technology, and scientific innovation. We are especially interested in understanding how Earth can help us prepare for future missions to the Moon and Mars. Our goal is to combine research, creativity, and technology to develop an innovative and scientifically meaningful solution to this challenge.
summary:
ISIDION is an interactive research platform that identifies and compares terrestrial environments that may help prepare for future human bases on the Moon and Mars. It examines candidate locations—including the Canadian High Arctic, Svalbard, the Danakil Depression, the Afar Volcanic Region, the Salar de Uyuni salt flats, and the Qaidam Basin—using geological, environmental, and operational characteristics.

ISIDION addresses the challenge by using Earth as a reference for understanding conditions future lunar and Martian missions may encounter. It compares candidate sites against the lunar south pole and Mars’s Jezero Crater using factors such as terrain, temperature, dust, water and ice, geology, biology, and field-testing feasibility. The project emphasizes process-based analogies rather than visual similarity and clearly identifies where each Earth analogy breaks down.

This project is important because well-characterized Earth analogs can help researchers test rover mobility, dust exposure, thermal cycling, drilling, biosignature detection, and mission operations before exploration begins. ISIDION makes these comparisons more accessible through an interactive map, analog fingerprints, and location profiles, supporting safer and better-informed planning for future Moon and Mars exploration. The project uses NASA’s MODIS vegetation data and Mars 2020 MEDA environmental data to support its comparisons.
details:
We also have a website unable to link along with our github repo so I'll be linking it here - https://isidion.netlify.app

ISIDION is a Python program that was built to help NASA find the best places on Earth to test space rovers and equipment alike before deploying them. Scientists often are forced to choose on visual similarity, but we wanted to bring a system to that process by using real math and elevation data instead. Visual similarity can be useful but ISIDION can whittle it down to a few options, rather than thousands of different places. Using Python, rasterio, and numpy alongside development support from Gemini and Copilot, our code takes open NASA satellite maps of Earth and the Moon, lines up their coordinate systems, and scans the land in grids to compare elevation, slope, and roughness. The locations are scored on a weighted error formula, where lower scores represent higher similarity. Because our program has the ability for high scale and high accuracy it had a tendency to crash our computers due to low RAM so we balanced speed with accuracy using downsampling techniques. The key thing here is that these settings are all able to be altered to the user's liking. ISIDION isn’t limited to any one data set. ISIDION’s versatility is what makes it special, allowing it to run anywhere at whatever level of accuracy you want.
